theme_evidence.claim: Creative output rises when a place concentrates capable people tackling related problems; innate ability alone does not substitute for proximity to an active peer cluster.
Ecosystem builders should treat hotspots as interacting communities rather than isolated talent pools, because distance from active centers sharply limits otherwise strong contributors.
The essay argues that capped outcomes reduce willingness to fund and found risky companies, and hypothesizes that the most uncertain startups would disappear first.
Idea-producing ecosystems combine exposure to emerging technology with trusted peers who can challenge and refine nascent concepts; universities are one implementation, not the only one.
Search for a formation bottleneck where a small, precisely targeted intervention can activate many capable would-be founders and produce companies that otherwise would not form.
A technology region needs both capable builders and experienced startup investors who contribute selection judgment, counsel, connections, and attentive capital.
A durable hub compounds over years as employees become founders and successful founders become investors; initial expert density must cross a self-sustaining threshold.
Test policy by replaying real founding histories under local rules, then remove incorporation, zoning, or compliance barriers that would eliminate fragile early companies.
Early founders who remain after success seed later companies with angel capital and encouragement, creating an organic flywheel whose cycle should be measured in years.
Regional density improves a startup's access to specialized expertise, recruits, supporting services, sympathetic norms, and high-value chance encounters.
The sharp geographic falloff in startup formation indicates that hub conditions combine to materially affect company survival and growth.

Low startup costs permit formation almost anywhere, yet in-person knowledge exchange and investor access can still improve outcomes; highly mobile seed teams may therefore strengthen established hubs while draining would-be regional centers.
Regional advantage increases with accumulated startup know-how, specialized participants, and concentrated face-to-face market activity rather than appearing only at a single threshold.
A strong hub combines investors able to assess unusual opportunities with a dense specialist market, so ecosystem quality includes judgment and operating knowledge as well as capital supply.
Concentrated peers and an interested audience provide encouragement and discovery channels that are difficult to recreate in fields where talent and new work are hard to evaluate.
Local norms materially shape sustained ambition, so an ecosystem must make startup work socially valued rather than expect isolated founders to overcome persistent indifference.
Startup methods flourish less readily where institutions and social norms resist autonomous, measurable small teams, even when the technical model is understood.

Public programs that cannot evaluate startups should borrow credible specialist selection, test a bounded cohort, preserve founder autonomy, and avoid ceremonial infrastructure or restrictive program rules.
Regional startup density can reinforce itself: a deliberate experiment must be large enough to form a functioning community and must account for local conditions.

Creating more startups differs from anchoring them locally because young teams are mobile; retention mandates select weaker applicants, while missing local investor expertise creates a reinforcing ecosystem bottleneck.

Policy should target the binding constraint on company formation, use recognized private investors as an eligibility signal when government lacks selection expertise, and begin with a limited, measurable trial.
Immigration restrictions can shrink the available founder pool and suppress new-company formation, including the downstream employment those companies could generate.
Model a prospective hub as a threshold system: founders, investors, and strong institutions must reinforce one another while established centers compete for the best new companies.
Treat startup formation as a social-capability problem requiring local expertise, not as infrastructure that policy or fast communication can reproduce on command.
Build enough participant density and variety that founders encounter specialized help and the community's ambitions become a supportive local norm.
Diagnose a hub by its people-driven mechanisms: social permission makes founding feel plausible, while repeated informal encounters connect teams with unusually relevant help.
Keep access open to exceptional international talent because strong peers attract one another and can compound into a dominant technical cluster.
In a connected, transparent, unpredictable network, information about mistreatment travels and consistent conduct earns durable trust.

Remove concrete city friction for talent-attracting amenities, make universities excellent talent magnets, preserve room for side projects, and tolerate unconventional people instead of staging generic entrepreneurship programs.
Confirm a young-talent foothold, then cultivate a patient flywheel in which companies remain locally, successful founders become investors, and the investor base grows organically.
Build founder-support institutions from problems founders have experienced directly, then use cohorts and alumni networks to reduce isolation, share assistance, and seed customer relationships.
